  `decode_graph_url` tool), transform the rows, and emit a new link. Prefer
  restructuring into named definitions: e.g. given `y = x^2 - 2x`, "add a
  tangent line at x = 3" becomes
  `f(x) = x^2 - 2x; g(x) = d/dx f(x); a = 3; y = f(x); y = f(a) + g(a)(x - a)`
  — with `a` as a draggable slider so the point of tangency stays explorable.
- Prefer a slider constant (`a = 1; ...`) when the user may want to explore a
  parameter, and `t` when they ask for animation.
- The graph state lives entirely in the link, and the link is the interface.
  The only server endpoints are /mcp (an MCP server that validates equations
  and emits links) and /api/og (link-preview images).
- If you are unsure whether a form is supported, emit the link anyway.
  Unsupported input fails loudly and visibly (an inline error on the offending
  row), never silently — so a graph either renders correctly or tells the user
  what to fix. There is no wrong-but-silent output to worry about.

- [Implicit grapher](https://equation.io/implicit/): plot an equation without solving for y
- [Slope field calculator](https://equation.io/slope-field/): y′ = f(x,y), click to trace
- [Complex function plotter](https://equation.io/complex/): f(w), domain coloring, conformal maps
- [Source code](https://github.com/aantthony/equation.io): open source (MIT); bug reports via GitHub issues

## Regression

Write `P = [(0,1),(1,3),(2,5),(3,7)]; P.y ~ m P.x + b` to fit a line through
the points: `P.x` and `P.y` are their coordinates, paired point by point.
(Write the data as points, or as columns of one CSV file: two separately
defined lists `X = […]`, `Y = […]` are independent, so `(X, Y)` would plot
their grid.) The left side is a numeric list (defined above the fit), an
explicit list, or a CSV column. The right side is a model over equally long lists, or a
scalar broadcast to the observations. Unbound scalar names are fitted
coefficients; already defined constants stay fixed. Data and fixed constants
must be static and defined above the fit. Coefficients are reusable values:
`y = m x + b` draws the model, `f(x) = m x + b` names it, and
`(P.x, P.y - f(P.x))` draws residuals. No fit settings exist outside the equations.

Examples: `P.y ~ a P.x^2 + b P.x + c` (polynomial), `P.y ~ a exp(b P.x)` (nonlinear),
`data.height ~ m data.age + b` (CSV). A fit row reports coefficients, RMSE,
R² when the observations have nonzero variance, and observation count.
Changing fixed constants or data refits the model. Missing/nonfinite pairs
are skipped with a visible count. Unequal lengths, rank-deficient models,
and too few finite observations are errors. At most 8 coefficients and
10,000 observations, or 2,000 observations for nonlinear models.
Nonlinear models must be differentiable in fitted coefficients; bounded,
deterministic multistart fitting reports a local fit or an error, not a
guaranteed global optimum. Fitting does not depend on t or simulation states.

`X ~ Normal(...)`, `X ~ Uniform(...)`, `X ~ Exponential(...)`, and the
unambiguous family names (`ChiSquared`, `StudentT`, `LogNormal`, `Cauchy`,
`Weibull`) retain their random-variable meanings. `Gamma`, `Beta` and `T`
follow the `exp` rule below — over a declared data list they are a model
(`Y ~ gamma(a X)`, `Y ~ beta (X - 1)`); with an undeclared left-hand name
they declare a random variable. Bare distribution aliases are case-insensitive,
including `exp`/`EXP`. For a declared data list, `Y ~ exp(a X)` is an
exponential regression model in any capitalization; with an undeclared
left-hand name, `Z ~ exp(2)` declares an exponential random variable.
Missing CSV data stays device-local in MCP and
previews, including curves that depend on its fitted coefficients. Fits over
literal data and their model curves work in shared links and static previews.

## Labels

`label(point, "text")` writes text beside a point on the graph, in the row's
color. Use it as a whole row. Examples:

    label((2, 4), "the curves cross here")
    A = (1, 1)
    label(A, "vertex")
    a = 2
    label((a, a^2), "moves with the slider")

The point may be a tuple, a named point, or point arithmetic, in 2D or 3D, and
may use constants, sliders, states, and `t`; it cannot use free x/y/z or u/v.
The text is plain and fixed. The MCP classifies these rows as `label`; static
previews draw the other rows but leave label text out (see preview_omits).

## Motion trails

`trail(A)` leaves a live trail of a point's observed positions, with a dot at
its current position. Use it as a whole row. Examples:

    A = (cos(t), sin(t))
    trail(A)

    trail((cos(t), sin(t), t/5))

A named 2D point, point arithmetic such as `trail(2A)`, or a 2D/3D vector state
can be traced. Components may use constants, sliders, states, and `t`; they
cannot use free x/y/z or u/v. `trail(cos(t), sin(t))` is equivalent to the
parenthesized tuple spelling. Matrix `trace(M)` keeps its existing meaning
(the sum of the diagonal), including inside other expressions.

The live browser retains at most 30 seconds and 2048 samples per trail,
sampling at most 60 times a second. Undefined positions or pauses over half a
second break the line instead of joining unobserved motion. Editing equations
or restarting the simulation clears history; framing/comment edits preserve
it. Trails start afresh on opening a graph and are not saved in shared URLs.
The MCP classifies these rows as `trail`; static previews use the fallback
card because a still image cannot reproduce accumulated live history.
